title: Record the stance: path validation does not enforce issuance-profile MUSTs or process the trust anchor
description:
Triage of all 49 x509-limbo ground-truth disagreements found zero defects in pkix-path. 47 of them fall into three classes that each want a recorded stance, so the question stops being re-litigated per testcase.

CLASS 1 -- issuance-profile MUSTs, 36 cases. RFC 5280 and the CABF Baseline Requirements both carry rules of the form 'conforming CAs MUST ...'. A validator that rejects a chain because its issuer broke an issuance rule is doing lint work inside path validation. §6.1 does not ask for it, and this workspace has pkix-lint and pkix-lint-cabf for exactly this.

  22 webpki::      all CABF: 7.1.2.1.3 root AKI fields (5), 7.1.4.3 CN-must-match-SAN
                   (9), 7.1.2.7.8/.11 basicConstraints and keyUsage (2), 6.1.5 RSA key
                   size (2), 7.1.2.5.2 empty NameConstraints (2), AIA syntax (1),
                   SAN criticality (1)
  14 rfc5280::     AKI critical or missing (3), SKI critical or missing (3), empty CA
                   subject, empty EKU, leaf cA=FALSE with keyCertSign=TRUE,
                   NameConstraints in an EE cert (2), malformed leading-period dNSName
                   constraint, non-critical SAN with empty subject, underscore in a
                   dNSName SAN

CLASS 2 -- trust-anchor processing, 5 cases. §6.1 processes the certificates in the path; the anchor is an input, and the algorithm never examines its own extensions or validity. So an expired root, a root missing or non-critically marking basicConstraints, a root with cA=TRUE and keyCertSign=FALSE, and a root bearing an unrecognised critical extension all validate here.

  rfc5280::validity::expired-root
  rfc5280::root-missing-basic-constraints
  rfc5280::root-non-critical-basic-constraints
  rfc5280::root-inconsistent-ca-extensions
  rfc5280::unknown-critical-extension-root

This is the class most worth a deliberate answer, because 'the operator chose this anchor' is a decent argument for ignoring its contents and a poor one for ignoring its validity dates.

CLASS 3 -- EKU chaining, 6 cases. All six bettertls::pathbuilding disagreements are one shape: an intermediate whose extKeyUsage is id-kp-emailProtection issuing a leaf whose extKeyUsage is id-kp-serverAuth. Browsers and rustls-webpki treat an intermediate's EKU as constraining what it may issue for; RFC 5280 does not chain EKU at all, and neither does OpenSSL -- it passes all six, as pkix-path does. So on this one the harness's own external oracle agrees with us and limbo's ground truth is the outlier.

  bettertls::pathbuilding tc5 tc12 tc38 tc44 tc71 tc77

The remaining 2 are harness limitations, tracked elsewhere: rfc5280::eku::ee-wrong-eku (PKIX-bnh7, the corpus states an EKU the loader ignores) and rfc5280::nc::nc-forbids-same-chain-ica (PKIX-t0w4, the positional-chain limitation already in INTEROP §6 -- and the only one of the 49 where pkix-path is the stricter party).

What to decide:

1. Classes 1 and 3 as deliberate divergences, documented, with the lint layer named as where those rules live. My recommendation. For class 1 the stronger follow-up is to route these testcases through the CABF and RFC 5280 lint oracles in the harness, so they are scored against the layer that owns them instead of counted as path-validation failures -- that turns 36 phantom disagreements into real lint coverage.
2. Class 2 needs its own answer, and the honest split may be to keep ignoring the anchor's extensions while checking its validity dates. That is a behavioural change and a divergence from the literal §6.1 reading, so it is a stance, not a bug fix.

Once recorded, INTEROP.md gains an entry per class and the disagreement count stops being read as 49 outstanding defects.
